open-question.question: In the rewritten enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md, is the enumerator told to first identify the axes of the decision and derive the options from them, or are distinctness and coverage stated only as properties the finished set must have?

Does the enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md carry its own explicit instruction to weigh the direction of not doing the thing the question is about, or is that direction left to follow from the general coverage requirement?
open-question.alternative: Step 2 of alternatives-procedure.md gets its own instruction, separate from the general coverage requirement, telling the enumerator to weigh the direction of not doing the thing the question is about on every question. The enumerator lists that direction as an option when it is honestly viable and leaves it out otherwise, with no dedicated place to record that it was considered. It targets the gap the benchmark aggregate names as the most frequent missing direction. The goal calls out this direction by name. The procedure's current requirement that the set be "complete now" already implied coverage and still missed it in practice, so a separate instruction is the most likely to change what the enumerator produces. It singles out one direction among the many the coverage rule is supposed to reach. Because it applies to every question, it pulls against the procedure's existing ban on strawmen and padding: the enumerator may add a token "don't do it" option where no one would really choose it. The block also has nowhere to record that the direction was weighed and rejected.

Step 2 states the general coverage requirement (the set covers the underlying decision, not the question's wording) and names not doing the thing, where honestly viable, as an example within that same sentence, following the goal's own parenthetical. There is no separate instruction and no check the enumerator must run on every question. It makes the most frequently missed direction visible where the enumerator reads the coverage rule, without adding a special-case rule or a per-question step. The procedure stays one general principle, and the wording tracks the goal closely. An example inside a general rule is weaker than an instruction and can be skimmed past. If the rewritten wording is not enough, the milestone's one-off re-run may still show sets that miss the direction, which weakens the case that the change is verified.

Step 2 states only the general coverage requirement, that the set covers the underlying decision rather than the question's wording. Dropping the thing is never mentioned and is expected to follow from applying that requirement. It keeps the enumeration rules to general principles with no special cases, so the procedure does not privilege one direction and adds no pressure to pad sets with a "don't do it" option where it isn't viable. The existing requirement that the set be "complete now" was already general and still let this direction go missing more often than any other, so relying on generality alone may not change behaviour. Whether this option is enough depends on how strongly the separately open rules on premise rejection and axis identification are written.

open-question.question: Does the enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md tell the enumerator to find what the question's wording takes for granted and weigh rejecting it, or is covering the underlying decision stated without such a step?
When several candidate options are one approach at different degrees or parameter values, how does the alternative set represent that approach?

Once an option's what-it-is text must also state where the option stands on each axis, does that field of alternatives-procedure.md keep its one-sentence limit, get a different stated limit, or carry no limit?

Is postponing the decision, leaving the question unanswered for a later milestone, a direction an alternative set may list, as distinct from the direction of not doing the thing the question is about?

When an axis of the underlying decision is already the subject of a sibling open question, does an alternative set's coverage extend to that axis, or does the existing rule that an option answering a sibling is left to that sibling bound it?
open-question.alternative: Keep the existing step-1 rule as the limit on coverage. The set covers only the axes of the underlying decision that no sibling question owns, so no option varies on a sibling-owned axis, and each option's what-it-is text states its position only on the axes this question owns. Each axis is decided in exactly one block. This keeps the rule that siblings supply scope and are never assumed settled, which is what lets the alternatives pass annotate blocks in parallel. It also keeps sets small, so one-axis-per-question authoring actually limits growth. Where a sibling-owned axis constrains this one, no set shows which pairings are unviable. The 12 historical overrides that took a combination on an axis the set never laid out could still fall between two questions, because each block's coverage stops at the boundary.

Retire the rule that an option answering a sibling is left to that sibling. Every axis of the underlying decision is laid out and each option states where it stands on it, including axes a sibling question also owns. This is the most literal reading of the goal's "cover the underlying decision" and "every combination weighed" requirements. Each set becomes a complete map of the decision, so an answer taking a cross-question combination can always find it listed. The same axis gets decided in two blocks. Recording one question's answer can fix a stance on a sibling's axis and conflict with that sibling's later answer, which causes more strip-and-re-run cascades. Stating a position on a sibling axis also comes close to presuming how that sibling settles, which step 2 forbids. Sets grow in exactly the way one-axis authoring is meant to prevent.

Siblings still bound the set, so no option varies on a sibling-owned axis. But the enumeration step now explicitly requires each option to name any sibling-owned axis its viability depends on, stated as a condition in its drawback without naming the expected outcome. This turns today's optional "say so in its drawback" into a required statement. It shows interdependence across questions without duplicating any decision. The recommendation pass gets the constraint in the option text, where it can become a depends-on tag. The block format needs no set-level statement, which the tool would refuse anyway. Unviable pairings are described one option at a time rather than laid out as combinations, so a combination spanning two questions is still never an option anyone can pick. It also adds a duty the enumerator must remember for every option, and the drawback field gets longer.

Siblings bound coverage by default. The one exception is a sibling-owned axis that constrains this question's axis so that not every pairing is viable: then the set lays out the viable combinations across both axes, and each option states its position on both. It targets the missed-combination failure without duplicating independent sibling decisions. Fuller coverage applies only where a single-axis set would really mislead. The enumerator has to judge interdependence per question, a conditional rule that is harder to apply the same way every time. Where it applies, it brings back the double-decided axis and the answer-time conflicts. Its merit turns on how the question of authoring interdependent axes settles, since that question decides whether such pairs reach two blocks in the first place.

open-question.question: What test does review-milestone-requirements apply when authoring a question to decide that a gap holds more than one axis and must be authored as several questions?
When two choices in one gap constrain each other so that not every pairing is viable, does review-milestone-requirements author them as two one-axis questions or as one multi-axis question?
How is the one-axis authoring rule of review-milestone-requirements verified, given that the milestone's one-off check re-runs only the alternatives pass?
Which of the historical cases whose alternative set missed the direction the answer took does the one-off check re-run: every case rated a strong candidate, or a smaller fixed subset?

Does the one-off check also re-run control cases, where the historical alternative set already contained the direction the answer took, to see that the new rules neither lose that direction nor pad the set?
Does the one-off check also run the unchanged enumeration rules on the same cases with the same model, so that a difference in the result can be attributed to the new wording and not to the model?
Where does the one-off check run the alternatives pass so that each case is grounded in its historical project state while the repositories the cases come from receive no commits or other changes?
Who decides whether a re-run alternative set contains the direction the historical answer took: the agent carrying out the check, or the user reviewing the sets?
What share of the re-run cases must contain the previously missing direction for the one-off check to count the change as verified?
If the one-off check falls short of its bar, does the milestone revise the enumeration wording and re-run the check, or record the shortfall and finish?

Which documents outside core/ are updated to match the new enumeration and authoring rules, among docs/skill-reference.md, claim 4 of docs/design-claims.md with its count of two to four alternatives, and CLAUDE.md?
Does CLAUDE.md gain an invariant entry explaining why alternative sets must be distinct and covering and why the count guideline is gone, or does the procedure's own wording carry that alone?
